newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Excommunicated Sri Lanka priest fights Church move.
newsitem.headline: Excommunicated Sri Lanka priest fights Church move.

text.p: A Sri Lankan Roman Catholic priest excommunicated by the Vatican last week demanded on Monday that the Church withdraw the move, saying it was null and void because he never committed heresy.
"I firmly state that I have never denied, rejected or deviated from any doctrine of the Catholic faith," Father Tissa Balasuriya, 72, told a news conference in Colombo.
"It follows that I have not committed any form of heresy. Therefore, there is no basis in fact or in law to make a declaration that I have incurred excommunication latae setentiae," Balasuriya said.
"Latae setentiae" is the severest form of excommunication in the Roman Catholic Church. It does not require a court of inquiry.

Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, who heads the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the Roman Catholic Church's doctrinal watchdog body, said in a Vatican statement on January 5 that Balasuriya incurred the severest form of excommunication because he distorted Catholic dogma.

The dispute stems from Balasuriya's 1990 book "Mary and Human Liberation". The author, a Catholic priest of 51 years and respected in Sri Lanka for his grassroot ties and so-called "Liberation Theology", challenges fundamental Catholic beliefs like baptism, original sin and immaculate conception.

Appearing in a white Catholic priest's robe, the elderly Balasuriya told the news conference that he had signed, of his own free will, a solemn "Profession of Faith" of Pope Paul VI to confirm his faith. Paul VI headed the Church between 1963 and 1978.

But the Vatican ordered him to sign a different profession, which he said deleted a paragraph from Pope Paul VI's document which lay open the chance of non-Christians to be saved in heaven and added what he called a "gender discrimination" that the Church could not ordain women into priesthood.
He said he did not sign the new profession, which was specifically drafted by the Vatican for him.

Despite the Vatican's claims that there was intensive dialogue with him over the matter in the past six years, Balasuriya said he was never given a fair hearing or trial. A 55-page document he wrote to defend his book was returned with one word of comment, "Unsatisfactory", Balasuriya said.
He said he has appealed the decision to the Vatican's supreme ecclesiastical court and that there would be an international signature campaign for Pope John Paul II to withdraw the act.
